slot.brief: Numerical where a fixed half-life must be used to find the time for a sample to fall from an initial to a final mass/activity — count the number of half-lives and multiply.

stem: A first-order reaction has a half-life of $15\ \text{min}$. The time required for the mass of the reactant to decrease from $64\ \text{g}$ to $2\ \text{g}$ is:

verdicts.working: 64 g → 2 g is a factor of 32 = 2^5, i.e. 5 half-lives. For first order, t = 5 × 15 min = 75 min.

working:
For a first-order process, the amount of reactant remaining after $n$ half-lives is given by:
$$\dfrac{m_t}{m_0} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^n$$

Given $m_0 = 64\ \text{g}$ and $m_t = 2\ \text{g}$:
$$\dfrac{2}{64} = \dfrac{1}{32} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^5$$

Therefore, the number of half-lives is $n = 5$.

The total time required is:
$$t = n \times t_{1/2} = 5 \times 15\ \text{min} = 75\ \text{min}$$

draft.distractor_notes:
Option A ($45\ \text{min}$) corresponds to $n = 3$ half-lives, resulting from incorrectly associating the reduction factor with $2^3$ or stopping at $8\ \text{g}$.
Option B ($60\ \text{min}$) corresponds to $n = 4$ half-lives, an off-by-one error where the decay is stopped at $4\ \text{g}$.
Option D ($90\ \text{min}$) corresponds to $n = 6$ half-lives, an off-by-one error where an extra half-life is counted (reducing down to $1\ \text{g}$).
